鐘琴以琴棒敲擊金屬片發聲。初學可先認清琴鍵排列：水平擺放時低音在左、高音在右；軍: The glockenspiel sounds when mallets strike metal bars. A beginner can start by learning the layout of the bars: laid out horizontally, the low notes are on the left and the high on the right; when a marching band sets the instrument vertically in front of a stand, the low notes are at the bottom and the high at the top, and the bars run across. Playing usually uses hard, non-metal mallets; metal mallets give a brighter tone and rubber ones a warmer tone, though a mallet that is too soft will not set the metal ringing. Four mallets can play chords, and the source mentions the Stevens grip. The bell lyre can be carried vertically on the shoulder and played with a single mallet; another kind rests on the shoulder and, laid horizontally, is played with two.
鐘琴為體鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號111.212，地區屬歐洲／: The glockenspiel is an idiophone, Hornbostel-Sachs number 111.212, its region Europe / Germany. Early forms sounded with small tuned bronze bells struck by a drumstick; in the seventeenth century metal bars replaced the bells, in the eighteenth a keyboard drove hammers against the underside of the bars, and in the nineteenth players took up mallets, at the same time as the Romantic period. From the middle of the nineteenth century the bell lyre was used in German military and folk music, and it later appears in the marching bands of Britain, the USA, Canada, the Philippines and Colombia.
鐘琴發聲體為固定音高金屬片，來源載明為鋁或鋼；早期形式以調音青銅鈴發聲，後改為金: The sounding bodies are metal bars of fixed pitch, which the source gives as aluminium or steel; early forms sounded with tuned bronze bells and later with metal bars. The mallets are mostly of hard materials, including metal (usually brass or aluminium) or polymers (Lexan, acrylic, phenolic, nylon), and rubber mallets can be used too. As for the stand, the body, the frame and other parts, the source does not state their materials.
鐘琴的清脆高音常見於管弦樂團、管樂隊、行進樂隊與流行音樂。在英國、美國與加拿大，: The glockenspiel's bright high notes are common in symphony orchestras, wind bands, marching bands and pop music. In Britain, the USA and Canada its variant, the bell lyre, is mostly used in marching bands, and in Germany it has been used in military and folk bands since the middle of the nineteenth century. In the Philippines all-percussion and lyre bands make it their main instrument, and it often appears in Colombian marching-band music. When listening, notice the bright melody it makes when hard mallets strike the metal bars, and how the tone changes depending on whether it is set vertically or horizontally in a marching band.
鐘琴音色清脆明亮，具有晶瑩剔透的金屬質感，音響穿透力強，能在樂隊中清晰突出。其音: The glockenspiel's timbre is crisp and bright, with the clear, transparent quality of metal; it carries well and stands out plainly in an ensemble. Its range is high, usually working in the treble, and the tone is light and mobile. The glockenspiel sounds as an idiophone: the metal bars themselves are the vibrating body and sound directly, the resonance is short, and each note is separate and full. Compared with the warm thickness of the xylophone, the glockenspiel is colder and sharper; compared with the piano its tone is clearer and plainer. Struck, the notes have a rounded, jewel-like quality, moderate in volume yet expressive. This particular sound makes the glockenspiel especially suited to brilliant, light-footed melodic passages, and in an orchestra it usually provides points of colour and emphasis.
鐘琴（Glockenspiel）為歐洲／德國的體鳴敲擊樂器，H-S編號111.2: The glockenspiel is a struck idiophone from Europe / Germany, H-S number 111.212, in the metal-bar class. Its metal bars of fixed pitch, of aluminium or steel, are laid out like a keyboard on a stand, and the player strikes them with hard metal or plastic mallets. Its tone is clear and high, and it is common in symphony orchestras, wind ensembles, marching bands and pop music; in a marching band it can be set vertically or horizontally.
